chapter_theme: Pattinathar's fourth agaval, the Kachchi Thiruvagaval, one unit addressed to the men who, having won a human birth among the seven, do not bow at the feet of Uma's lord but delight in women. The poet takes the stock praise of the female body limb by limb, soles like cotton, shins like leaping fish, thighs like plantain stems, belly like a banyan leaf, breasts like lotus buds, hands like kanthal, neck like areca, mouth like the murukku flower, teeth like pearls, nose like the kumizh, eyes like lilies, ears like vallai stalks, hair like a dark cloud, and sets against each the sweat, bone, excrement, mucus, wax and lice it covers; then names the vulva as the gate of hell the praisers desire, the field where embryos grow, the way of the menstrual flow, the sore covered with a cloth, the great road by which every man and woman is born, and tells them not to call it sweet but to worship the twin feet of the one Lord of Kachi, who pities a devotee even for a leaf, and to stop praising the women of pleasure.
structure_note: An exordium naming the audience (மானிடர்க் கெல்லாம் யானெடுத் துரைப்பேன்; விழிவெளி மாக்கள் தெளிவுறக் கேண்மின்), the catalogue of limbs from the sole upward to the hair, each in the pattern 'the X that does Y, they call Z', a second catalogue of some twenty names for the female organ in -வழி and -வாயில், and a closing call to the Lord's feet. The ascent from feet to hair reverses the head-to-foot (கேசாதிபாதம்) order of courtly praise.

303.reading: To all the men who, born human among the seven births that Brahma, son of Vishnu, arranged, do not bow at the flower feet of the mountain daughter's lord and reach the Siva-state but delight in women and celebrate love, the poet speaks, and bids the blind-eyed listen: the soles that toil over thorns and stones they call cotton; the shins that are white bone they praise as leaping varal fish; the thighs of flesh and bone they call plantain stems; the waist that carries the long body they call a drum; the belly rolling with excrement, urine, slime and wrinkles they call a banyan leaf; the breasts that spread like a spider's web, swell, ooze, are scratched by nails, dry, shrink and hang for people to laugh at they call lotus buds, 'I say this to the blind of lust'; the hands that stretch, fold, take goods, feed and knead they call kanthal flowers; the neck of sweat and grime they call the areca palm; the hot and foul mouth they call the murukku flower; the teeth that chew rice and curry they call pearls; the sharp nose that drips water and mucus they call the kumizh fruit; the eyes that run with water and rheum they call water-lilies; the ears where wax rots they praise as vallai stalks; the hair on the skull, where lice and nits breed if oil is not combed in, they call a dark cloud; and saying such things in praise they go to the gate of hell they desire, the pit of lust where skin and flesh ooze pus, the field where embryos grow, the way the menstrual flow passes, the holed gate, the great road down which the eight-span body comes, the hidden place where earthly lust is spent, the gate where the dog of lust sits desiring, the sluggish road where those without the grace of the moon-crested one linger, the sore they cover with a cloth saying 'this is a wound', the rich sore that sounds with running water, the way the deluded enter and the sick never leave, the pit the proud lechers fall into, the great road by which woman and man are born, the water gate beside the gate where excrement falls: do not say this is sweet; bow instead at the twin feet of the one Lord of Kachi, who pities his devotees even for an offered leaf and grants the release of the Siva-state, lord of release, ageless First, who saw all the worlds in all the eggs, and give up praising the women of pleasure.
303.nuance: The method is to quote the convention and then name the referent: each limb is given first as function or matter (bone, sweat, mucus) and then as the poets' figure, so that the figure is convicted by what it covers. The second catalogue is unusually literal, and தூமைக் கடவழி, the way of the menstrual flow, uses the Siddhars' word for the womb's impurity; பெண்ணும் ஆணும் பிறக்கும் பெருவழி concedes that the same gate is the way of every birth, including the hearer's. The attack is on the eye and the convention, not on women as persons, though the text does not make that distinction itself. சிலந்தி போலக் கிளைத்து, spreading like a spider or its web, for the breasts' first growth is obscure; இடைகழி வாயில் is the vestibule gate. பச்சிலை இடினும், even for a green leaf offered, is the standard measure of the Lord's easy grace.

links.note: The Naladiyar lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinew, skin and flesh and asks which of them is the garlanded woman; Pattinathar goes limb by limb and sets bone, sweat, mucus and wax against the flower and fruit each is called. Both dissolve the praised woman into her matter; Pattinathar does it against the poets' conventions by name.

Arunagirinathar repeats the questions men ask, whether the eyes are vel or carp, the hair cloud or forest, the breasts Meru or tusks, and asks not to drown in such women's eyes; Pattinathar repeats the same conventions (cloud for hair, lily for eyes, lotus bud for breasts) and answers each with the body's matter. Both quote courtly praise in order to refuse it.

On the reading in which Sivavakkiyar rebukes those who count the breast that grew and rose as maya and tells them instead to examine the body of the jiva that holds grace, Pattinathar is the man rebuked: he strips the breast and every limb down to bone and pus and the womb's impurity. The conflict depends on that reading of 1372's first line; if its கொங்கை is a figure for pride, the two do not meet.

source_issues: Line 19 சிலந்தி போலக் கிளைத்துமுன் னெழுந்து is obscure as a figure for the breasts; the word may be corrupt.
Line 32 உள்ளுங் குறும்பி யழுகுங் காதை (the ear where wax rots) is the only limb given without a stated function; the construction is otherwise uniform.
The unit is headed நான்காவது கச்சித் திருவகவல் and counted with the three Koyil Thiruvagavals though addressed to Kachi (Kanchipuram), not Tillai.
